components.text: Whether sensitivity-based religious skepticism destroys epistemic closure.
Whether a method fits facts and discriminates among comparably compatible rival explanations.
Whether the sensitivity objection defeats religious skepticism through closure.
Whether criticism of sensitivity can substitute for positive justification and evidence for belief in God.
Whether the domino model establishes an impossible infinite causal past.
Whether the model establishes characteristics of a conscious divine cause.
The domino inference depends on a fictional one-directional infinite timeline rather than establishing the relevant cosmological model.
Known time and causality appear contained within the universe, so their extension beyond it requires support.
Whether a first cause must exist outside time and in every possible world.
Whether the conclusion follows from explicit premises rather than assertion.
The necessity of an atemporal God in every possible world requires a stated premise-and-conclusion demonstration.
Whether necessity across possible worlds has been proved by stated premises.
Whether the fictional infinite-timeline model establishes a first cause.
Every imaginable world is said necessarily to possess a first cause, making that cause axiomatic.
The response generalizes the first-cause claim beyond the particular domino timeline to any imagined world.
Whether calling a first cause axiomatic supplies evidence for its truth.
Whether the affirmative case provides a demonstrated argument for God.
Assuming a proposition as necessary does not constitute an argument or evidence that the proposition is true.
Whether axiomatic first-cause reasoning establishes God without evidence.
Identify a particular detectable miracle and establish a reasonable connection between it and divine causation.
Identify a particular miracle offered as evidence of divine activity.
Provide a reasonable evidential basis attributing that event to a god.
The resurrection is identified as the particular miracle and historical substantiation is offered as its evidential basis.
Whether axiomatic acceptance establishes the particular first-cause God claim.
Whether the affirmative has supplied discriminating evidence for its specific religious conclusion.
Incompatible gods and non-gods can be axiomatically accepted by the same procedure, so the procedure cannot discriminate truth.
The response reiterates the need for good evidence but does not examine the resurrection's historical warrant.
Whether axiomatic starting points can yield discriminating good evidence.
Whether the proposed standard distinguishes competing explanations.
Whether axiom status itself constitutes evidence for the starting proposition.
Evidence anchored in a genuine axiom is claimed to avoid an endless regress of justificatory questions.
A valid implication from an axiom to a derivative proposition is offered as a model of good argument.
Whether resurrection evidence is historically substantiated and attributable to divine action.
Extraordinary experience reports can be culturally shaped and fallible rather than independently verified divine evidence.
The comparison emphasizes ordinary evidential assessment rather than axiomatic exemption.
Whether the argument distinguishes a specific God from incompatible alternatives.
Whether experience narrows the argument toward a particular religious tradition.
The argument's conclusion is limited to deism or classical monotheism rather than a uniquely Christian God.
The scope concession avoids relying on culture-specific experience to establish Christianity.
Whether extraordinary reports are fallible culturally shaped interpretations rather than verified evidence.
Whether a particular miracle is identified and reasonably attributed to God.
Reasonably credible testimony is admissible evidence even when the event was not personally or sensitively verified.
The move defends admitting miracle testimony but does not identify or attribute a particular miracle.
Whether God may receive a special axiomatic evidential status.
Whether parsimony consistently narrows generic theism toward one God.
Whether testimony is evaluated under shared evidential standards.
Miracle testimony and God claims should face the same consistently applied evidence evaluation used for competing beliefs.
Granting God axiomatic status is identified as a special exemption rather than consistent evidential evaluation.
Occam's razor is invoked against unnecessary multiplication, though the exact scope argument is not fully examined.
Whether an ultimate cause has characteristics that entail conscious divine agency.
Whether the proposed divine characteristics follow from an explicit argument.
If the ultimate cause's reason for acting were external, that external factor would instead be the ultimate cause.
The internal source is said to imply conscious will, but modal necessity is not independently proved.
The move supplies a causal inference but does not compare it under shared standards with impersonal alternatives.
Whether the theistic axiom differs epistemically from arbitrary incompatible assumptions.
Whether axiom status supplies warrant rather than merely naming an assumption.
Whether a non-special criterion distinguishes genuine axioms.
An axiom is distinguished from a presupposition by being self-evident, irreducible, and self-authenticating.
The response supplies a conceptual distinction but does not show that God's existence satisfies the axiom criteria.
The distinction could be consistently applied only with an independent test for self-evidence, which is not supplied.
Whether theistic and scriptural claims are assessed under shared consistent standards.
Literal extermination is said to conflict with the command to drive the same population away, supporting a hyperbolic reading.
Whether there is a principled basis for treating destruction texts as hyperbole.
Whether resurrection is treated literally under the same interpretive standard.
Whether scriptural interpretation bears on the proposed axiom distinction.
A principled method is required to distinguish literal resurrection from figurative killing or slavery passages.
The resurrection's literal treatment is compared with other passages, though its historical evidence is not directly examined.
The remark does not address the conceptual axiom-presupposition distinction.
